transcript:
[00:00] Sara Liang: Hi everyone, thanks for joining, uh, we'll run about an hour, quick intros.
[00:08] Priya Menon: Hi, Priya here, Head of ML at AtlasMorph. We're re-architecting our chat infra for product launch Q3.
[00:15] Ethan Cole: Ethan, SRE — concerned primarily about p95 latencies and burst concurrency.
[00:20] Lina Zhao: Lina, platform eng, will own deployment decisions.
[00:25] Mateo Ruiz: Mateo, Redwood SE, nice to meet you all. Quick agenda: understand traffic/profile, goals, then mapping to hosting modes and benchmark plan.
[00:36] Priya: Great. To start, our main goal: sub-second perceived latency for our streaming assistant. We want p95 perceived under 500ms for 90% of interactions, and under 200ms for quick question flows.
[00:46] Ethan: But we also have bursts — black friday style — where concurrent open sessions spike to around 600 to 800 concurrent streams for ~20 minutes.
[00:54] Sara: Okay that's helpful, and what's your typical token distribution? average prompt length, completion tokens?
[01:02] Priya: Median prompt tokens ~25, median completion ~40, tail sometimes 400–800 tokens for long form. Our 95th percentile completion length is about 280 tokens.
[01:12] Lina: We also rely on streaming to send incremental tokens, so server-to-client chunk latency matters, not just total generation time.
[01:18] Mateo: Right. From Redwood side, streaming latency depends on model choice, KV cache behavior, and batching policy. For hosted, we have optimized kernels and multi-tenant pooling which helps cold-starts but at heavy bursts you'll get queuing unless you use dedicated capacity.
[01:34] Priya: Can you quantify — like p95 for streaming for a 40-token response on hosted vs dedicated?
[01:40] Mateo: Ballpark: on our verifed medium models, hosted p95 for short streaming chunks might be ~120–180ms single-turn if under moderate load; with burst concurrency and multi-tenant noise that can degrade to 300–450ms unless you reserve dedicated GPUs. Dedicated pools with pinned instances reduce queuing and tail to ~80–160ms p95 for similar workloads.
[01:56] Ethan: That's a wide range. How does KV prefix caching help with that?
[02:00] Mateo: If you can prefix-cache the KV for common context (session prompts), you bypass repeated decoder overhead when clients re-open, so the per-token latency drops significantly on warm hits — sometimes 30–40% reduction for long context. But cache footprint and hit rate matter.
[02:16] Priya: We have many short sessions with similar templates, so hit rate could be decent.
[02:20] Sara: For benchmarking, we'll want to capture both cold and warm scenarios. We'll also run token/sec microbenchmarks — end-to-end with network RTT similar to your infra.
[02:29] Lina: About hosting modes: our compliance requires VPC peering and KMS integration, and some customers insist on on-prem in the future. How feasible is private deployment?
[02:38] Mateo: Private (VPC/private deployment) is supported — we offer customer-managed VPC with private control plane and KMS/HSM integration. On-prem is more involved but doable for enterprise licenses. You give up some of our pooled infra optimizations but gain isolation and direct network paths.
[02:53] Ethan: Ok, then it's between dedicated (predictable p95 but costlier) and private (isolated but more ops). Can Redwood autoscale for bursts in dedicated?
[03:02] Mateo: Yes, dedicated supports autoscaling policies and burst capacity; you can configure headroom and burst units. For very spiky patterns we recommend a committed baseline plus burst pool to avoid cold starts.
[03:12] Priya: We need guidance: cost vs latency tradeoffs. Could you provide a spreadsheet with sample scenarios?
[03:17] Sara: Yes — I'll send a cost-latency spreadsheet mapping tokens/sec and concurrency to expected cost for hosted vs. dedicated.
[03:23] Ethan: For the lab benchmark, what should we provide?
[03:26] Mateo: Ideally: a 7-day traffic histogram, sample prompts (anonymized), and a small client load generator that reproduces open streaming sessions. We'll run microbenchmarks: single-stream latency, multi-stream concurrency, and token/sec sustained throughput to map GPU saturation.
[03:40] Priya: What about quantized models or 4-bit flavor to save cost? Any p95 impact?
[03:45] Mateo: Quantization can reduce latency on certain hardware and lower memory, but you may see small quality differences. For throughput, int8/4-bit often increases token/sec; for latency p95 it helps if the kernel path is optimized. We'll recommend profiles per model.
[03:58] Lina: Network RTT — should we simulate our cross-region users? We have EU users pinging our US region with ~140ms RTT.
[04:05] Mateo: Yes simulate RTT. Client-perceived p95 is local RTT plus server generation p95 plus chunking overhead. For EU users, the network portion will dominate; we can recommend regional hosts or multi-region failover.
[04:16] Priya: Any out-of-the-box tooling for token accounting and tracing?
[04:20] Sara: Redwood Console gives token-level cost and latency breakdowns, per-route dashboards, and tracing hooks you can instrument into your client. We'll show you during the lab.
[04:30] Ethan: Security checklist — SOC2, SSO/SAML, audit logs, KMS?
[04:34] Sara: We have SOC2 Type II, SAML SSO integrations, RBAC, and audit logs. KMS integrations available for private and dedicated. We'll attach a short security pack.
[04:43] Priya: Competitors: we ran some initial tests on Anthropic and MosaicML; Mosaic had good multi-GPU throughput, Anthropic better tail for some flows. How does Redwood compare?
[04:54] Mateo: We try to optimize kernel selection, batching strategy, and KV cache to reduce tails. We can produce a benchmark runbook and compare apples-to-apples if you can share the prompt sets.
[05:05] Lina: One of our constraints is restart resilience — sessions must not lose context if a node goes down. How does Redwood handle falling back?
[05:12] Mateo: We have automated fallback to compatible model variants and region failover. For dedicated private deployments you can configure replication and stateful cache sync strategies.
[05:22] Priya: For the planned lab, can we run a 2-hour soak where we peak to 700 concurrent streams and measure p95 over time?
[05:28] Mateo: Yes, that's the plan — we'll provision a dedicated pool or simulate load on hosted with reserved burst; we'll instrument p50/p95/p99 and the per-token throughput.
[05:36] Ethan: Any gotchas — e.g., batching that increases tail when you enable multiplexing?
[05:40] Mateo: Yes — batching increases throughput but can hurt strict p95 for single-stream latency if you pile too many requests into a batch. We configure adaptive batching to respect latency SLOs — smaller batches for short prompts, larger for long running completions.
[05:54] Priya: Good. Also curious about prefix caching and session affinity, we use session stickiness now.
[05:59] Mateo: Session affinity with warm caches reduces p95; we can recommend cache TTLs and eviction policies.
[06:05] Sara: Quick recap and next steps — we'll share benchmark guide, security docs, and cost spreadsheet. AtlasMorph will share traffic samples and schedule lab window.
[06:15] Priya: Perfect. Thanks all.
[06:18] Lina: Thanks.
[06:20] Ethan: Thanks, talk soon.
[06:24] Sara: Bye.

Notes: transcription includes some minor auto-caption errors; timestamps approximate. The call had some cross-talk near 03:00–03:20 when scheduling items.
